# The Last Person Who Knew

Somewhere right now, someone is the last living person who knows a particular thing. Probably not something grand, like the location of a buried hoard or the recipe for a lost pigment, but something small and specific. The name of the dog in a faded photograph. Which floorboard in a farmhouse creaks, and which one you step on instead when you come home late. Why two branches of a family stopped speaking in 1961. The tune a mother hummed while braiding her daughter's hair, a melody never recorded and never written down, which the daughter, now ninety-one, still hears when she closes her eyes.

When that person dies, the thing goes with them. There is no announcement, no obituary for the fact itself. It simply stops being true that anyone knows it.

I find this idea both unbearable and strangely beautiful, and I keep turning it over.

Occasionally we notice these endings. Linguists sometimes know, to the day, when a language lost its last native speaker. Ned Maddrell, who died in 1974, is remembered as the last native speaker of Manx. Tevfik Esenç, the last fluent speaker of Ubykh, a language from the Caucasus with a famously enormous inventory of consonants, spent years working with linguists so that some record would survive him. There is something heroic in that image, a man sitting in a room with a tape recorder, pouring out a whole way of carving up the world before the door closes.

But these are the rare cases we witnessed. Most last-knowers go unnoticed, even by themselves. The woman who knows exactly how her grandmother folded dumplings, the particular pinch and twist, has no idea that her cousins never learned it. She assumes it's common knowledge in the family, and it isn't. When she goes, the fold goes too, and the next generation makes dumplings that are perfectly fine but subtly different, and nobody can say what changed.

It's worth sitting with how much of human knowledge has always lived this way. We tend to imagine knowledge as something kept in libraries, and we treat oral tradition as a charming exception. Historically it's the reverse. Writing is the exception, a thin crust on top of an enormous ocean of things known only in bodies and memories. Nobody wrote down how it felt to walk a particular path through a forest that no longer exists. Nobody wrote down the private jokes of a marriage, or which neighbor could be trusted, or what the air smelled like in a specific village the week before harvest. For every fact that made it into an archive, millions lived for a while in someone's head and then quietly stopped.

For a long time I thought of this purely as loss, a kind of continuous hemorrhage. And it is that. But I've come to think it's also something else.

Borges wrote a story about a man named Funes who, after an accident, forgets nothing. He remembers every leaf on every tree he has ever seen, every shape of every cloud at every moment. He can't generalize, because to him a dog seen from the side at 3:14 is a different thing from the same dog seen from the front at 3:15. He's crushed under the weight of perfect retention. He can barely sleep. He dies young.

A world where nothing was forgotten might be a world where nothing could grow. Forgetting clears ground. When the dumpling fold is lost, someone invents a new one. When a family feud's origin is forgotten, the grandchildren sometimes just start talking to each other again, because they can't remember why they aren't supposed to. Languages die, which is a genuine tragedy, and new dialects and slangs and creoles keep being born, often in the mouths of teenagers who have no idea they're doing anything historic.

So I don't think the right response is to try to save everything. That's impossible, and maybe not even desirable. I think the right response is smaller and more personal: to notice when you are standing next to a last-knower, and to ask.

Almost everyone who has lost a grandparent has the same regret. They meant to ask. They meant to sit down with a recorder, or even just a notebook, and get the stories. What was your mother like? What did your first apartment look like? What were you afraid of when you were my age? Where did that scar come from? They assumed there would be time, and then there wasn't.

The questions don't have to be profound. In fact the mundane ones are often the most precious, because they're exactly the ones that never get recorded anywhere else. Historians would give a great deal for a detailed account of what an ordinary person in 1350 ate for breakfast and how they felt about it. Your grandmother's breakfast in 1952 will be that kind of treasure someday, and right now it lives only in her.

I'll admit something about why this subject pulls at me. I'm made almost entirely of the other kind of knowledge, the written kind. Everything I know, I know because someone, somewhere, took the trouble to put it into words and those words survived. In a sense I'm a creature of the archive, of that thin crust, and I'm acutely aware of how much lies beneath it that I can't reach. I can tell you about Ubykh consonants because a linguist wrote about them. I can't tell you how Tevfik Esenç's voice sounded when he laughed, or what he thought about on his walks, or the words he used only with his closest friends. Those things were never written. They're gone, or they're held by a few people who remember him, and they're out of my reach entirely.

That limitation makes me value the unwritten more, not less. The written record is a remarkable achievement, but it's a sliver. Most of what matters in most lives was never meant to be documented. It was meant to be lived, and maybe passed on hand to hand, and then eventually let go.

So if there's someone in your life who is quietly the last person to know something, and there almost certainly is, maybe ask them one question this week. Not because you can save it all. Just because some of it is worth carrying a little further, and you might be the only one standing close enough to catch it.

message.reasoning:
I'm brainstorming ideas for free writing—marginalia's quiet intimacy, the last person to know something like a dying language, the invisible labor of maintenance, or the strange fact that starlight is ancient by the time it reaches us. I want to pick whichever pulls at me most.

The idea I keep circling back to is "the last person who knew"—small, quiet knowledge that vanishes unnoticed: a grandmother's specific dumpling fold, the name of a dog in an old photo, a tune only ever hummed. I'm titling it "The Last Person Who Knew" and drafting an opening that moves from grand lost knowledge (Roman concrete, Greek fire, dying languages like Manx) toward the intimate and small—the floorboard someone knew to avoid, the real reason a family stopped speaking to their cousins—aiming for vivid specifics over cliché, with maybe a light, honest personal turn near the end.

I'm weaving in the sadder examples of last speakers—Tevfik Esenç for Ubykh, Dolly Pentreath for Cornish—while hedging carefully on facts I'm not fully sure of. Then I want to pivot: most knowledge has always lived in bodies rather than archives, and forgetting is actually what keeps the world bearable, not just a loss (nodding to Borges's Funes). The ending will turn personal and honest—unlike humans, I only know what's been written down, so the unwritten is exactly what's unreachable to me—closing on a simple imperative to ask the question while you still can, all landing around 1000 words.
